content: In September 2016, a scoping meeting was held to prioritize and draft critical questions and outcomes for digital health interventions. This was followed by a final meeting in June 2018 to review synthesized evidence and formulate recommendations. Online surveys were conducted before and after the September meeting to refine and prioritize the questions. The scoping process identified priority questions related to digital health interventions, which were included in the guidelines. These interventions were defined and categorized, such as digital birth notifications, which use technology to notify health systems of births, trigger birth registration and certification processes, and compile vital statistics. Similarly, digital death notifications support the reporting of deaths, including cause-of-death information, and facilitate death registration and certification. Other interventions include digital stock notifications and commodity management systems, which monitor and report stock levels of medical supplies. Provider-to-provider telemedicine enables health workers to consult with specialists or other providers for case management. Targeted client communication uses digital tools to deliver customized health information to specific population segments, such as reminders for appointments or health education messages. Health worker decision support systems combine patient data with clinical protocols to assist in diagnosis and treatment decisions. Digital tracking of patients’ health status and services allows health workers to follow up on care delivery, while mobile learning (mLearning) provides health workers with access to educational and training content. The guidelines emphasize the use of mobile devices for delivering these interventions, given their widespread availability and potential to improve service delivery, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The recommendations focus on ensuring patient safety, privacy, and data security, as well as the capacity of health systems to respond effectively to digital notifications and interventions. For example, the WHO recommends digital birth notifications in settings where health systems can respond to notifications by initiating postnatal services and ensuring birth registration. Similarly, digital death notifications are recommended in research contexts where health systems can validate and act on the data. Digital stock notifications are advised in settings with supply chain systems capable of timely responses to stock alerts. Provider-to-provider telemedicine is similarly recommended for improving case management through consultations between health workers. Targeted client communication is advised for addressing sensitive health issues, such as sexual and reproductive health, provided that privacy concerns are addressed. Digital decision support tools are recommended for health workers performing tasks within their defined scope of practice. Digital tracking of clients’ health status, combined with decision support and targeted communication, is recommended in settings where health systems can integrate these components effectively. The guidelines also recommend the digital provision of educational and training content to health workers to complement traditional methods of continued education and training. These interventions aim to strengthen health systems by improving accountability, supply chain management, service quality, and accessibility to health information and services. Digital health interventions are recognized as transformative tools for addressing health system challenges, such as geographic inaccessibility, low service demand, and delayed care provision. The WHO emphasizes the need for evidence-based digital health solutions to advance universal health coverage (UHC) and improve health outcomes globally.
